title: Operator decision lattice for prefix-cache failure and dashboard playbook
author: Aisha Martinez
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook gives operators a decision lattice plus a dashboard kit for diagnosing, mitigating and preventing serious failures in the runtime's KV/prefix cache layer (service: kv-prefix-cache). It ranks interventions so we keep SLOs (p95 < 150ms, availability 99.95%) while controlling cost and avoiding risky rollbacks that could corrupt data.

Scope
-----
- Components: kv-prefix-cache, runtime-router, request-batcher, model-variant-service, cache-reaper-job.
- Symptoms: eviction storms, rising miss ratio, KV replication lag, and operator misconfiguration causing cascading tail latency.
- Audience: platform operators, oncall engineers, runtime maintainers, product SREs.

Why a decision lattice?
----------------------
A linear runbook assumes one fixed sequence. Prefix-cache incidents depend on several correlated signals (latency, eviction rate, tenant priority, capacity headroom), so the lattice maps signals to a partial order of safe actions. Operators pick the highest-priority action that fits current telemetry, subject to safety invariants: no data loss, degrade gracefully, protect critical-tenant SLOs.

Key signals and thresholds
--------------------------
- prefix_cache_evictions_total (per-pool, 1m rate): GREEN < 10/m, YELLOW 10–100/m, RED > 100/m
- prefix_cache_miss_ratio (5m): GREEN < 0.08, YELLOW 0.08–0.25, RED > 0.25
- runtime_tail_p95_ms (global, 1m): GREEN < 150, YELLOW 150–300, RED > 300
- tenant_token_cost_rate_delta (1h, top tenants): GREEN < +20% baseline, YELLOW +20–100%, RED > +100%
- cache_reaper_backlog_count: GREEN < 500, YELLOW 500–5000, RED > 5000
- kv_replication_lag_seconds: GREEN < 2s, YELLOW 2–60s, RED > 60s

Decision lattice overview
-------------------------
A: Informational — dashboard context, runbook annotations.
B: Non-disruptive mitigations — throttle low-priority tenants, short-lived local caching, slightly larger batch window.
C: Capacity adjustments — temporary burst capacity, more cache pool workers, more memory headroom.
D: Controlled degradation — tenant slicing, soft-eviction for background tenants, shorter max sequence length for non-critical requests.
E: Failsafe swaps — lower-KV model variant, read-through fallback from regional caches.
F: Emergency teardown — drain/restart cache nodes, manual KV repair (high risk).

Order: A < B < C < D < E < F. Branches can run in parallel; e.g., with a tenant cost spike and low replication lag prefer B; with high replication lag hold off on C.

Playbook
--------
1) Triage (0–5 minutes)
   - Open the prefix-cache incident dashboard.
   - Is the spike global or limited to a region/pool?
   - `kubectl -n runtime get pods -l app=kv-prefix-cache` and `curl -s http://ops-api/internal/kv/cache-stats?pool=all`

2) Information collection (5–10 minutes) [A]
   - Post a summary with panel links in the incident channel.
   - Note the top-5 affected tenants by token_cost and error_rate.
   - Take a non-blocking heap/profile snapshot if safe.

3) Non-disruptive mitigations (10–25 minutes) [B]
   - `opsctl tenant throttle --tag background --rate 0.5x`
   - `opsctl cache tune --pool default --lru-window 2m`
   - Router batch_delay_ms +10ms for best-effort requests.
   - Watch 5–10 minutes; if latency and miss ratio recover, move to monitoring.

4) Capacity adjustments (25–60 minutes) [C]
   - Precondition: replication_lag_seconds <= 5s and burst headroom available.
   - `infractl instance-group scale --name kv-cache-burst --delta +4`
   - On Dedicated pools, route lower-priority traffic to the burst pool via runtime-router policy.
   - Watch backlog and eviction rate; plan permanent capacity or LRU tuning if it helps.

5) Controlled degradation (60–120 minutes) [D]
   - Move non-critical tenants to a soft-eviction class.
   - Set `max_seq_len.background = 512`.
   - Spot-check QPS-sensitive endpoints for core customers.

6) Failsafe swaps (120–180 minutes) [E]
   - Swap to a lower-KV variant (e.g., variant-quantized-v2).
   - Set `runtime-router.fallback.read_through = true` on affected routes.
   - Inform partner teams about degraded feature flags.

7) Emergency teardown (>=180 minutes) [F]
   - If kv_replication_lag_seconds > 120s or memory corruption is suspected, schedule a coordinated drain.
   - `kubectl cordon/drain`; bring up fresh nodes only after operator verification.
   - Manual KV repair follows the KV-repair playbook and needs Platform Lead and DB owner approval.

Dashboard kit
-------------
- Prefix Cache Overview: eviction rate per pool, miss ratio, memory utilization, active keys.
- Tail Latency by route: p50/p95/p99 heatmap.
- Tenant impact: top 10 tenants by error_rate and token_cost_delta.
- Replication health: lag_seconds, commit_errors, replica_count.
- Operator actions timeline: annotations stream.

Prometheus examples:
- Eviction rate: `increase(prefix_cache_evictions_total[1m]) / 60`
- Miss ratio: `sum(prefix_cache_misses_total[5m]) / sum(prefix_cache_requests_total[5m])`
- p95: `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le, route))`

Alerting rules
- ONSET_ALERT: prefix_cache_evictions_total_rate > 100/m sustained for 3m -> P2 -> steps 1–3
- DEGRADATION_ALERT: runtime_tail_p95_ms > 300ms for 2m -> P1 -> page
- REPLICATION_ALERT: kv_replication_lag_seconds > 60s for 2m -> P0 -> page platform-db and platform-ops
- COST_SURGE_ALERT: top-3 tenant_token_cost_rate_delta > 100% (1h) -> P2 -> coordinate with customer-success first

Oncall checklist
----------------
- [ ] Open the dashboard and read recent annotations.
- [ ] Set severity and initial notes.
- [ ] Check pods and backlog queues.
- [ ] Apply B-group mitigations if safe; observe 10m.
- [ ] Otherwise check preconditions and go to C or D.
- [ ] After E or F, notify platform leadership and customer success; prepare postmortem.

Safety rules
------------
- No emergency teardown (F) during a global network partition without Platform Lead approval.
- Throttle lower-priority tenants before restarting pools.
- Annotate expected traffic impact before any restart/drain.

Follow-up
---------
- Immediate: record timeline and lattice branches used.
- 1-week: replay in the staging degradation-lab.
- 1-month: evaluate more cache headroom and tenant-aware eviction.

Appendix: maintenance matrix
----------------------------
| Action                           | Impact scope    | Risk | Typical duration | Owner        | Approval needed? |
|----------------------------------|-----------------|------|------------------|--------------|------------------|
| Soft-throttle background tenants | background only | Low  | 5–10m            | platform-ops | No               |
| Spin burst workers               | pool-level      | Med  | 10–30m           | infra-team   | Ops Lead         |
| Apply tenant slicing             | tenant groups   | Med  | 10–30m           | runtime-team | Product SRE      |
| Drain cache node                 | pool node       | High | 30–60m           | platform-ops | Platform Lead    |

Appendix: commands
------------------
- `kubectl -n runtime get pods -l app=kv-prefix-cache -o wide`
- `curl -sS https://ops-api/internal/kv/cache-stats?pool=pool-1 | jq`
- `opsctl tenant throttle --selector tag=background --factor 0.5`
- `infractl instance-group scale --name kv-cache-burst --delta 4`

Ownership and SLAs
------------------
- Primary owner: Runtime platform team (runtime-platform@redwood.com).
- Secondary owner: Infra capacity team.
- Oncall: platform-ops.
- SLOs to protect: global p95 < 150ms, availability >= 99.95%.

Document maintenance
--------------------
- Review quarterly and after any incident reaching step D or above.
